claim: Sam68 (Khdrbs1) is strongly expressed in neurogenic areas of the neocortex.
source: We found that the RNA- binding protein Sam68 (Khdrbs1) is strongly expressed in neurogenic areas of the neocortex and supports the self-renewing potential of mouse NPCs.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, and it is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Sam68 supports the self-renewing potential of mouse NPCs.
source: We found that the RNA- binding protein Sam68 (Khdrbs1) is strongly expressed in neurogenic areas of the neocortex and supports the self-renewing potential of mouse NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by clonogenic assays and proliferation data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Knockout of Khdrbs1 constricted the pool of proliferating NPCs by accelerating their cell cycle exit and differentiation into post-mitotic neurons.
source: Knockout of Khdrbs1 constricted the pool of proliferating NPCs by accelerating their cell cycle exit and differentiation into post-mitotic neurons.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by BrdU labeling and Ki67 staining experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Sam68 function is linked to regulation of Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA 3'-end processing.
source: Sam68 function was linked to regulation of Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA 3'-end processing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through 3'-RACE experiments and CLIP assays in Figure 5.

claim: Binding of Sam68 to an intronic polyadenylation site prevents its recognition and premature transcript termination, favoring expression of a functional enzyme.
source: Binding of Sam68 to an intronic polyadenylation site prevents its recognition and premature transcript termination, favoring expression of a functional enzyme.
evidence: This mechanism is described in the abstract and supported by CLIP assays showing Sam68 binding to the cryptic PAS in intron 7 (Figure 5F) and 3'-RACE experiments (Figure 5D-E).

claim: Lower ALDH1A3 expression and activity in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs results in reduced glycolysis and clonogenicity.
source: The lower ALDH1A3 expression and activity in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs results in reduced glycolysis and clonogenicity, thus depleting the embryonic NPC pool and limiting cortical expansion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ALDH activity assays (Figure 6B), lactate production measurements (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2), and clonogenic assays (Figure 4B).

claim: Reduced ALDH1A3 expression and activity depletes the embryonic NPC pool and limits cortical expansion.
source: The lower ALDH1A3 expression and activity in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs results in reduced glycolysis and clonogenicity, thus depleting the embryonic NPC pool and limiting cortical expansion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements of cortical expansion (Figure 3D-E) and NPC numbers (Figure 2, Figure 3).

claim: Sam68 establishes a novel link between modulation of ALDH1A3 expression and maintenance of high glycolytic metabolism in the developing cortex.
source: Our study identifies Sam68 as a key regulator of NPC self-renewal and establishes a novel link between modulation of ALDH1A3 expression and maintenance of high glycolytic metabolism in the developing cortex.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing that ALDH1A3 modulation affects glycolytic metabolism (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Most neurons in the mouse developing brain are generated between E10 and birth.
source: In the mouse developing brain, most neurons are generated between the 10th day of embryonal life (E10) and birth (Martynoga et al., 2012), even though adult neurogenesis persists in restricted areas near the lateral ventricles, the ventricular (VZ) and subventricular (SVZ) zones (Bjornsson et al., 2015), and in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (Urbán and Guillemot, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Martynoga et al., 2012).

claim: Adult neurogenesis persists in restricted areas near the lateral ventricles (VZ and SVZ) and in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
source: In the mouse developing brain, most neurons are generated between the 10th day of embryonal life (E10) and birth (Martynoga et al., 2012), even though adult neurogenesis persists in restricted areas near the lateral ventricles, the ventricular (VZ) and subventricular (SVZ) zones (Bjornsson et al., 2015), and in the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (Urbán and Guillemot, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Bjornsson et al., 2015; Urbán and Guillemot, 2014).

claim: Neuroepithelial cells and radial glia cells divide symmetrically in the VZ to generate cells retaining self-renewal capacity, or asymmetrically to give rise to intermediate progenitor cells or differentiated cells.
source: As embryonic neurogenesis starts, neuroepithelial cells at first, and radial glia cells (RGCs) later, divide symmetrically in the VZ, to generate cells retaining self-renewal capacity, or asymetrically to give rise to intermediate progenitor cells (IPCs) or differentiated cells (Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; Taverna et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; Taverna et al., 2014).

claim: IPCs divide away from the VZ one or more times before they generate post-mitotic neurons, which localize in the basal compartment of the developing cortex.
source: IPCs divide away from the VZ, one or more times, before they generate post-mitotic neurons, which localize in the basal compartment of the developing cortex (cortical layer).
evidence: This is a description of the known developmental process, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Dysregulation of neurogenesis can result in developmental disorders linked to neurological pathologies.
source: Conversely, dysregulation of neurogenesis can result in developmental disorders linked to neurological pathologies (Sun and Hevner, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Sun and Hevner, 2014).

claim: Regulation of metabolic routes and gene expression cooperate to balance NPC self-renewal and differentiation during cortical expansion.
source: Multiple mechanisms, including regulation of metabolic routes (Shyh-Chang et al., 2013) and of gene expression (Paridaen and Huttner, 2014), cooperate to create an interconnected network that balances NPC self-renewal and differentiation in the correct time and space during cortical expansion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Shyh-Chang et al., 2013; Paridaen and Huttner, 2014).

claim: Modulation of RNA metabolism, particularly alternative splicing, plays a key role in neurogenesis and formation of neuronal circuits.
source: Mounting evidence documents that modulation of RNA metabolism, and particularly of alternative splicing, plays a key role in neurogenesis and during formation of neuronal circuits, as highlighted by the global changes in the splicing signature that accompany the transition from NPCs to neurons (Zheng and Black, 2013; Raj and Blencowe, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Zheng and Black, 2013; Raj and Blencowe, 2015).

claim: Brain is among the tissues displaying the largest extent of alternative splicing.
source: Notably, brain is among the tissues displaying the largest extent of alternative splicing, which likely contributes to the complexity of neural circuits (Raj and Blencowe, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Raj and Blencowe, 2015).

claim: A temporal switch in the expression of PTBP1 and PTBP2 governs splicing of a large set of neural-specific exons.
source: For instance, a temporal switch in the expression of two homologous polypyrimidine-tract-binding proteins, PTBP1 and PTBP2, governs splicing of a large set of neural-specific exons in genes involved in neuronal functions (Boutz et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Boutz et al., 2007).

claim: Knockout of the Ptbp2 gene caused premature neurogenesis and depletion of the NPC pool.
source: Knockout of the Ptbp2 gene caused premature neurogenesis and depletion of the NPC pool (Licatalosi et al., 2012), proving the crucial role played by this splicing factor in the developing brain.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Licatalosi et al., 2012).

claim: nSR100 regulates a network of exons in genes involved in neuronal functions and its knockout in mice leads to widespread neurodevelopmental defects.
source: Similarly, the neural-specific serine-arginine (SR)-related protein of 100 kDa (nSR100) regulates a network of exons in genes involved in neuronal functions and knockout of this gene in mice leads to widespread neurodevelopmental defects (Calarco et al., 2009; Quesnel-Vallières et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Calarco et al., 2009; Quesnel-Vallières et al., 2015).

claim: Sam68 is highly expressed in brain and testis.
source: Another splicing factor involved in neuronal functions is Sam68, encoded by the Khdrbs1 gene, which is highly expressed in brain and testis (Richard et al., 2005; Paronetto et al., 2009), and it was shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of fragile X tremor/ataxia syndrome (Sellier et al., 2010) and spinal muscular atrophy (Pedrotti et al., 2010; Pagliarini et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Richard et al., 2005; Paronetto et al., 2009).

claim: Sam68 is involved in the pathogenesis of fragile X tremor/ataxia syndrome.
source: Another splicing factor involved in neuronal functions is Sam68, encoded by the Khdrbs1 gene, which is highly expressed in brain and testis (Richard et al., 2005; Paronetto et al., 2009), and it was shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of fragile X tremor/ataxia syndrome (Sellier et al., 2010) and spinal muscular atrophy (Pedrotti et al., 2010; Pagliarini et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Sellier et al., 2010).

claim: Sam68 is involved in the pathogenesis of spinal muscular atrophy.
source: Another splicing factor involved in neuronal functions is Sam68, encoded by the Khdrbs1 gene, which is highly expressed in brain and testis (Richard et al., 2005; Paronetto et al., 2009), and it was shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of fragile X tremor/ataxia syndrome (Sellier et al., 2010) and spinal muscular atrophy (Pedrotti et al., 2010; Pagliarini et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Pedrotti et al., 2010; Pagliarini et al., 2015).

claim: Sam68 modulates splicing of the neurexin one gene (Nrxn1) in response to neuronal activity.
source: Furthermore, Sam68 modulates splicing of the neurexin one gene (Nrxn1) in response to neuronal activity (Iijima et al., 2011) and its ablation caused altered synaptic plasticity and motor coordination defects (Lukong and Richard, 2008; Iijima et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Iijima et al., 2011).

claim: Ablation of Sam68 caused altered synaptic plasticity and motor coordination defects.
source: Furthermore, Sam68 modulates splicing of the neurexin one gene (Nrxn1) in response to neuronal activity (Iijima et al., 2011) and its ablation caused altered synaptic plasticity and motor coordination defects (Lukong and Richard, 2008; Iijima et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Lukong and Richard, 2008; Iijima et al., 2011).

claim: Sam68 mRNA and protein levels peak between E13.5 and E15.5 in the mouse cortex.
source: Developmental analysis of the mouse cortex showed that Sam68 mRNA and protein levels peak between E13.5 and E15.5, whereas its expression slowly declines thereafter and is minimal from 9 days post-partum (9dpp) until adulthood (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Sam68 expression slowly declines after E15.5 and is minimal from 9 days post-partum until adulthood.
source: Developmental analysis of the mouse cortex showed that Sam68 mRNA and protein levels peak between E13.5 and E15.5, whereas its expression slowly declines thereafter and is minimal from 9 days post-partum (9dpp) until adulthood (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The peak of Sam68 expression corresponds to stages of intense neurogenesis in the developing cortex.
source: The peak of Sam68 expression corresponds to stages of intense neurogenesis in the developing cortex (Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; Taverna et al., 2014) and parallels that of the NPC marker SOX2, which is also high between E10.5 and E15.5 and sharply decreases in post-natal stages (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to support the timing of neurogenesis, and is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B showing parallel expression patterns of Sam68 and SOX2.

claim: SOX2 expression is high between E10.5 and E15.5 and sharply decreases in post-natal stages.
source: The peak of Sam68 expression corresponds to stages of intense neurogenesis in the developing cortex (Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; Taverna et al., 2014) and parallels that of the NPC marker SOX2, which is also high between E10.5 and E15.5 and sharply decreases in post-natal stages (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sam68 is strongly expressed in neurogenic periventricular regions of E13.5 brain.
source: Furthermore, Sam68 is strongly expressed in neurogenic periventricular regions of E13.5 brain, like SOX2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sam68 and SOX2 co-localized in most cells of the VZ and SVZ of E13.5 cortex.
source: Sam68 and SOX2 co-localized in most cells of the VZ and SVZ of E13.5 cortex (Figure 1D), and their expression was even more restricted to these cortical zones at 1dpp (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sam68 and SOX2 expression was even more restricted to VZ and SVZ cortical zones at 1dpp.
source: Sam68 and SOX2 co-localized in most cells of the VZ and SVZ of E13.5 cortex (Figure 1D), and their expression was even more restricted to these cortical zones at 1dpp (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Sam68 is abundant in proliferating NPCs and steadily decreases when cells are induced to differentiate.
source: Sam68, like SOX2, was abundant in proliferating NPC (0d) and steadily decreased when cells were induced to differentiate (1d-6d in Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-PCR, Western blot, and qPCR data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: Expression of the neuronal marker TUBB3 is barely detectable in proliferating NPCs and augments upon differentiation.
source: Conversely, expression of the neuronal marker TUBB3 (βIII-tubulin) was barely detectable in proliferating NPCs and augmented upon differentiation (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-PCR, Western blot, and qPCR data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: Proliferating cells (BrdU-positive cells) were significantly decreased in the cortex of Khdrbs1-/- embryos at E13.5.
source: Proliferating cells (BrdU-positive cells) were significantly decreased in the cortex of Khdrbs1-/- embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SOX2+-NPCs and SOX2+/BrdU+ cells were markedly reduced in E13.5 Khdrbs1-/- cortex.
source: Likewise, SOX2+-NPCs, as well as the number of NPCs undergoing DNA synthesis (SOX2+/BrdU+ cells), were also markedly affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that fewer NPCs are present and proliferate in the E13.5 Khdrbs1-/- cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Total and proliferating RGCs (PAX6+ and PAX6+/BrdU+ cells) were markedly reduced in the Khdrbs1-/- cortex at E13.5.
source: Strikingly, total (PAX6+ cells) and proliferating RGCs (PAX6+/BrdU+ cells) and IPCs (TBR2+ and TBR2+/BrdU+ cells) were markedly reduced in the knockout cortex (Figure 2B,C), whereas differentiated neurons (TBR1+ cells) were almost doubled (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Total and proliferating IPCs (TBR2+ and TBR2+/BrdU+ cells) were markedly reduced in the Khdrbs1-/- cortex at E13.5.
source: Strikingly, total (PAX6+ cells) and proliferating RGCs (PAX6+/BrdU+ cells) and IPCs (TBR2+ and TBR2+/BrdU+ cells) were markedly reduced in the knockout cortex (Figure 2B,C), whereas differentiated neurons (TBR1+ cells) were almost doubled (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Differentiated neurons (TBR1+ cells) were almost doubled in the Khdrbs1-/- cortex at E13.5.
source: Strikingly, total (PAX6+ cells) and proliferating RGCs (PAX6+/BrdU+ cells) and IPCs (TBR2+ and TBR2+/BrdU+ cells) were markedly reduced in the knockout cortex (Figure 2B,C), whereas differentiated neurons (TBR1+ cells) were almost doubled (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No TBR1-positive cell was labeled by BrdU in both wild-type and knockout embryos at E13.5.
source: No TBR1-positive cell was labeled by BrdU in both wild-type and knockout embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), confirming that these cells are post-mitotic neurons (Englund et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, with a citation to support the interpretation.

claim: The fraction of NPCs that exited the cell cycle (Ki67-/BrdU+/BrdU+ cells) in the E12.5-E14.5 time-frame was significantly increased in Khdrbs1-/- embryos.
source: Co-staining with the Ki67 proliferation marker revealed that the fraction of NPCs that exited the cell cycle (Ki67-/BrdU+/ BrdU+ cells) in the E12.5-E14.5 time-frame was significantly increased in Khdrbs1-/- embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In wild-type embryos, approximately 30% of post-mitotic neurons were labeled with BrdU in the E12.5-E14.5 time-frame.
source: Furthermore, in wild-type embryos, ~30% of post-mitotic neurons were also labeled with BrdU (Figure 3C), indicating that only a subset of NPCs underwent terminal differentiation within 48 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In Khdrbs1-/- embryos, more than 80% of TBR1-positive cells were labeled with BrdU in the E12.5-E14.5 time-frame.
source: By contrast, this process was strongly enhanced in knockout embryos, with more than 80% of TBR1-positive cells that were labeled with BrdU (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BrdU-positive proliferating cells were strongly decreased in Khdrbs1-/- cortex at E17.5.
source: A 2-hr pulse showed that BrdU-positive proliferating cells were strongly decreased in Khdrbs1-/- cortex also at this stage, which was reflected in lower number of SOX2-positive NPCs (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: SOX2-positive NPCs were reduced in Khdrbs1-/- cortex at E17.5.
source: A 2-hr pulse showed that BrdU-positive proliferating cells were strongly decreased in Khdrbs1-/- cortex also at this stage, which was reflected in lower number of SOX2-positive NPCs (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Cortical expansion, measured as length from ventricular to pial surface, was significantly reduced in E17.5 Khdrbs1-/- embryos.
source: Furthermore, although they were indistinguishable in size from the wild type and heterozygote littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), cortical expansion, measured as length from ventricular to pial surface, resulted significantly reduced in E17.5 Khdrbs1-/- embryos (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by measurements shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Khdrbs1-/- embryos were indistinguishable in size from wild type and heterozygote littermates at E17.5.
source: Furthermore, although they were indistinguishable in size from the wild type and heterozygote littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), cortical expansion, measured as length from ventricular to pial surface, resulted significantly reduced in E17.5 Khdrbs1-/- embryos (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by weight analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockout neurospheres grew at slower rate than wild type ones.
source: We observed that knockout neurospheres grew at slower rate than wild type ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), even though no differences were detected in the extent of cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and appeared irregular in shape with a tendency to form protrusions, due to cells that attached to the substrate and exited the sphere (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by neurosphere diameter measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No differences were detected in the extent of cell death between wild type and knockout NPCs.
source: We observed that knockout neurospheres grew at slower rate than wild type ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), even though no differences were detected in the extent of cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and appeared irregular in shape with a tendency to form protrusions, due to cells that attached to the substrate and exited the sphere (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell death analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockout neurospheres appeared irregular in shape with a tendency to form protrusions due to cells that attached to the substrate and exited the sphere.
source: We observed that knockout neurospheres grew at slower rate than wild type ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), even though no differences were detected in the extent of cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and appeared irregular in shape with a tendency to form protrusions, due to cells that attached to the substrate and exited the sphere (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by bright field images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When seeded at single cell level, knockout NPCs produced cytoplasmic extensions and attached to the plate, while wild-type cells remained in suspension.
source: Furthermore, when seeded at single cell level, knockout NPCs produced cytoplasmic extensions and attached to the plate, while wild-type cells remained in suspension (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The clonogenic potential of wild-type NPCs slowly declined from approximately 45% to approximately 25% after 7 passages in culture.
source: The clonogenic potential of wild-type NPCs slowly declined from ~45% to~25% after 7 passages in culture. However, loss of clonogenicity was markedly accelerated in knockout NPCs, reaching ~10% by passage 7 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of clonogenicity was markedly accelerated in knockout NPCs, reaching approximately 10% by passage 7.
source: The clonogenic potential of wild-type NPCs slowly declined from ~45% to~25% after 7 passages in culture. However, loss of clonogenicity was markedly accelerated in knockout NPCs, reaching ~10% by passage 7 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Khdrbs1-/- NPCs differentiated with higher efficiency than wild-type cells, as indicated by fewer cells retaining high expression of PAX6 and Nestin after 1 day.
source: Khdrbs1-/- NPCs differentiated with higher efficiency than wild-type cells, as indicated by the fewer cells that retained high expression of the stemness markers PAX6 and Nestin after 1 day (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: After 3 days of differentiation, Khdrbs1-/- NPCs gave rise to significantly more neurons and oligodendrocytes than wild-type NPCs.
source: When differentiation was evaluated after 3 days, Khdrbs1-/- NPCs gave rise to significantly more neurons and oligodendrocytes than the corresponding wild-type NPCs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: Neurons generated by knockout NPCs exhibited higher complexity and more advanced differentiation stage, as documented by their increased branching level.
source: Furthermore, neurons generated by knockout NPCs exhibited higher complexity and more advanced differentiation stage, as documented by their increased branching level (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Splicing-sensitive exon arrays identified 254 annotated genes regulated at the expression levels in knockout NPCs.
source: Splicing-sensitive exon arrays identified 254 annotated genes regulated at the expression levels and 117 exons in 87 genes regulated at the splicing level in knockout NPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Splicing-sensitive exon arrays identified 117 exons in 87 genes regulated at the splicing level in knockout NPCs.
source: Splicing-sensitive exon arrays identified 254 annotated genes regulated at the expression levels and 117 exons in 87 genes regulated at the splicing level in knockout NPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Sam68 generally acted as a repressor of expression and the majority of targets were upregulated in knockout NPCs.
source: Sam68 generally acted as a repressor of expression and the majority of targets were upregulated in knockout NPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Sam68 functioned as splicing enhancer for target exons.
source: By contrast, Sam68 functioned as splicing enhancer for target exons, with little overlap between genes regulated at expression and splicing level (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: There is little overlap between genes regulated at expression and splicing level by Sam68 in NPCs.
source: By contrast, Sam68 functioned as splicing enhancer for target exons, with little overlap between genes regulated at expression and splicing level (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: Exon cassette was the predominant splicing event regulated by Sam68 in NPCs, followed by alternative last exon selection.
source: Exon cassette was the predominant splicing event regulated by Sam68 in NPCs, followed by alternative last exon selection (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Gene ontology analysis highlighted significant enrichment of functional categories related to neuron and oligodendrocyte properties.
source: Notably, gene ontology analysis highlighted significant enrichment of functional categories related to neuron and oligodendrocyte properties (cluster 1 in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), thus supporting the pro-differentiation effect of Sam68 depletion in NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The 5' region of the Aldh1a3 transcript (exons 1–7) was upregulated in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: The 5' region of the Aldh1a3 transcript (exons 1–7) was upregulated in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs, whereas the 3' region (exons 8–13) was downregulated (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The 3' region of the Aldh1a3 transcript (exons 8–13) was downregulated in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: The 5' region of the Aldh1a3 transcript (exons 1–7) was upregulated in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs, whereas the 3' region (exons 8–13) was downregulated (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by microarray and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 3'-RACE experiments revealed usage of an alternative PAS in intron 7 of Aldh1a3 that is followed by two potential cleavage sites.
source: Sequencing of the 3'-RACE products amplified in knockout NPCs revealed usage of an alternative PAS in intron 7 that is followed by two potential cleavage sites (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by 3'-RACE PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Incubation of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs with DRB showed that the amplicon corresponding to exon 7-intron 7 sequences was stable up to 6 hr of incubation.
source: Furthermore, incubation of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs with 5,6-dichloro-1-β-D-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB) to block RNA transcription led to rapid decay of transcripts containing exon 3-intron 3 and intron 8-exon 8 sequences, indicative of pre-mRNA amplification, whereas the amplicon corresponding to exon 7-intron 7 sequences was stable up to 6 hr of incubation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-PCR data after DRB treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CLIP experiments showed strong recruitment of Sam68 in proximity of the cryptic PAS in intron 7 of the Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA.
source: In line with this possibility, UV crosslink immunoprecipitation (CLIP) experiments showed strong recruitment of Sam68 in proximity of the cryptic PAS in intron 7 of the Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA, whereas binding in other regions was much weaker (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by CLIP assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Sam68 binding in regions of Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA other than intron 7 was much weaker.
source: In line with this possibility, UV crosslink immunoprecipitation (CLIP) experiments showed strong recruitment of Sam68 in proximity of the cryptic PAS in intron 7 of the Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA, whereas binding in other regions was much weaker (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by CLIP assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed the reduction of the full-length ALDH1A3 protein in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed the reduction of the full-length ALDH1A3 protein (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A truncated ALDH1A3 protein (ALDH1A3△) originating from the ALE in intron 7 was not detected in NPCs.
source: However, we did not detect a band corresponding to the truncated protein (ALDH1A3△) originating from the ALE in intron 7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Blocking the proteasome by incubation with MG132 did not lead to ALDH1A3△ accumulation.
source: Blocking the proteasome by incubation with MG132 did not lead to ALDH1A3△ accumulation, whereas interference with autophagy using chloroquine caused a mild accumulation of a protein product slightly smaller than the recombinant ALDH1A3△ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Interference with autophagy using chloroquine caused a mild accumulation of a protein product slightly smaller than the recombinant ALDH1A3△.
source: Blocking the proteasome by incubation with MG132 did not lead to ALDH1A3△ accumulation, whereas interference with autophagy using chloroquine caused a mild accumulation of a protein product slightly smaller than the recombinant ALDH1A3△ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Full-length ALDH1A3 overexpressed in HEK293 exhibited enzymatic activity.
source: Full-length ALDH1A3 overexpressed in HEK293 exhibited enzymatic activity, as measured by reduction of NADPH (Lindahl et al., 1982), whereas the ALDH1A3△ protein was completely inactive (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ALDH1A3△ protein was completely inactive.
source: Full-length ALDH1A3 overexpressed in HEK293 exhibited enzymatic activity, as measured by reduction of NADPH (Lindahl et al., 1982), whereas the ALDH1A3△ protein was completely inactive (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ALDH1A3△ efficiently co-immunoprecipitated with full-length ALDH1A3.
source: ALDH1A3△ efficiently co-immunoprecipitated with ALDH1A3. However, its co-expression with the full-length protein reduced ALDH activity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Co-expression of ALDH1A3△ with the full-length protein reduced ALDH activity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: ALDH1A3△ efficiently co-immunoprecipitated with ALDH1A3. However, its co-expression with the full-length protein reduced ALDH activity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ALDH activity was markedly decreased in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: In line with the reduced expression of full length ALDH1A3, ALDH activity was markedly decreased in Khdrbs-/- NPCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ALDEFLUOR assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ALDH1A3 staining was significantly reduced in E13.5 knockout embryos with respect to wild-type littermates.
source: Furthermore, ALDH1A3 staining, which is restricted to the SOX2+ cells in VZ and SVZ of the developing cortex, was also significantly reduced in E13.5 knockout embryos with respect to wild-type littermates (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ALDH1A3 staining is restricted to the SOX2+ cells in VZ and SVZ of the developing cortex.
source: Furthermore, ALDH1A3 staining, which is restricted to the SOX2+ cells in VZ and SVZ of the developing cortex, was also significantly reduced in E13.5 knockout embryos with respect to wild-type littermates (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The full-length Aldh1a3 transcript rapidly declined upon differentiation of wild-type NPCs in culture.
source: The localization of ALDH1A3 suggests that its expression is restricted to RGCs. Moreover, we found that the full-length Aldh1a3 transcript rapidly declined upon differentiation of wild-type NPCs in culture (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The decline in full-length Aldh1a3 transcript upon NPC differentiation was accompanied by reduced Sam68 expression and increased expression of ALDH1A3△.
source: Importantly, this decline was accompanied by reduced Sam68 expression and increased expression of ALDH1A3△ (Figure 6D), indicating that alternative 3'-end processing of the Aldh1a3 transcript is a physiological process of NPC differentiation controlled by fluctuations in Sam68 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is a highly significant correlation between expression of Sam68 and Aldh1a3 in post-natal brain.
source: In agreement with a direct modulation of Aldh1a3 expression by Sam68, we also observed a highly significant correlation between expression of these genes in post-natal brain, with highest levels of both transcripts in olfactory bulb and cerebellum and lowest expression in the hypothalamus (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expression of full-length Aldh1a3 transcript was reduced in olfactory bulb and cerebellum of Khdrbs1-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, expression of full-length Aldh1a3 transcript was reduced in olfactory bulb and cerebellum of Khdrbs1-/- mice, while the ALE-containing shorter transcript was induced (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The ALE-containing shorter Aldh1a3 transcript was induced in olfactory bulb and cerebellum of Khdrbs1-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, expression of full-length Aldh1a3 transcript was reduced in olfactory bulb and cerebellum of Khdrbs1-/- mice, while the ALE-containing shorter transcript was induced (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Expression of GFP-ALDH1A3 almost completely rescued the growth and clonogenic defects of knockout NPCs.
source: Notably, expression of GFP-ALDH1A3 almost completely rescued the growth and clonogenic defects of knockout NPCs (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by neurosphere growth and clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 7A, 7B, and 7C.

claim: Expression of ALDH1A3△ in wild-type NPCs blocked proliferation and interfered with formation of neurospheres.
source: In line with its negative effect of ALDH activity, expression of ALDH1A3△ in wild-type NPCs blocked proliferation and interfered with formation of neurospheres, even though the cells remained alive (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by neurosphere growth data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous ALDH1A3 in wild-type NPCs promoted neuronal differentiation to an extent similar to that observed in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: Moreover, knockdown of endogenous ALDH1A3 in wild-type NPCs promoted neuronal differentiation to an extent similar to that observed in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by differentiation assay data shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: Glycolytic activity was significantly reduced in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs compared to wild-type cells.
source: Lower accumulation of the end-product lactate in the culture medium indicated that glycolytic activity was significantly reduced in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs compared to wild-type cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Inhibiting ALDH activity using DEAB reduced lactate production in NPCs.
source: A similar reduction in lactate production could be obtained by inhibiting ALDH activity using N,N-diethylaminobenzaldehyde (DEAB) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), a commonly used inhibitor of ALDH enzymes (Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Knockdown of Aldh1a3 expression in wild type NPCs reduced anaerobic glycolysis to the levels of knockout cells.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of Aldh1a3 expression in wild type NPCs was sufficient to reduce anaerobic glycolysis to the levels of knockout cells, whereas overexpression of GFP-ALDH1A3 fully rescued lactate production in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-ALDH1A3 fully rescued lactate production in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of Aldh1a3 expression in wild type NPCs was sufficient to reduce anaerobic glycolysis to the levels of knockout cells, whereas overexpression of GFP-ALDH1A3 fully rescued lactate production in Khdrbs1-/- NPCs (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Reduced glycolytic activity accompanied differentiation of NPCs in vitro.
source: Notably, reduced glycolytic activity accompanied differentiation of NPCs in vitro (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C), concomitant with the decline in Sam68 and Aldh1a3 expression (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lactate production measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of ALDH activity with 50 µM DEAB in wild-type NPCs recapitulated the neurosphere growth defect of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: Strikingly, pharmacologic inhibition of ALDH activity in wild-type NPCs was sufficient to recapitulate the neurosphere growth (Figure 7G) and clonogenic defect (Figure 7H) of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by neurosphere growth data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of ALDH activity with 50 µM DEAB in wild-type NPCs recapitulated the clonogenic defect of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
source: Strikingly, pharmacologic inhibition of ALDH activity in wild-type NPCs was sufficient to recapitulate the neurosphere growth (Figure 7G) and clonogenic defect (Figure 7H) of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Sam68 is physiologically required for adipogenesis.
source: Analysis of the mouse knockout model revealed that Sam68 is physiologically required for adipogenesis (Richard et al., 2005; Huot et al., 2012), male and female gametogenesis (Paronetto et al., 2009; Bianchi et al., 2010; Paronetto et al., 2011) and for regulation of synapse morphology and function in neurons (Iijima et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Richard et al., 2005; Huot et al., 2012).

claim: Sam68 is physiologically required for male and female gametogenesis.
source: Analysis of the mouse knockout model revealed that Sam68 is physiologically required for adipogenesis (Richard et al., 2005; Huot et al., 2012), male and female gametogenesis (Paronetto et al., 2009; Bianchi et al., 2010; Paronetto et al., 2011) and for regulation of synapse morphology and function in neurons (Iijima et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Paronetto et al., 2009; Bianchi et al., 2010; Paronetto et al., 2011).

claim: Sam68 is physiologically required for regulation of synapse morphology and function in neurons.
source: Analysis of the mouse knockout model revealed that Sam68 is physiologically required for adipogenesis (Richard et al., 2005; Huot et al., 2012), male and female gametogenesis (Paronetto et al., 2009; Bianchi et al., 2010; Paronetto et al., 2011) and for regulation of synapse morphology and function in neurons (Iijima et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Iijima et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2013, 2015).

claim: Khdrbs1-/- mice displayed high perinatal lethality.
source: Notably, Khdrbs1-/- mice also displayed high perinatal lethality (Richard et al., 2005), but the biological processes and the genes regulated by Sam68 during embryonic development are completely unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Richard et al., 2005).

claim: ALDH1A3 was shown to support self-renewal and clonogenic potential of cancer stem cells.
source: Indeed, ALDH1A3 was shown to support self-renewal and clonogenic potential of cancer stem cells (Duan et al., 2016), including glioma stem cells (Mao et al., 2013), which can differentiate into neurons and glial cells like NPCs (Lathia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Duan et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2013).

claim: Glioma stem cells can differentiate into neurons and glial cells like NPCs.
source: Indeed, ALDH1A3 was shown to support self-renewal and clonogenic potential of cancer stem cells (Duan et al., 2016), including glioma stem cells (Mao et al., 2013), which can differentiate into neurons and glial cells like NPCs (Lathia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Lathia et al., 2015).

claim: The canonical PAS sequences (AAUAAA and AUUAAA) correspond to optimal binding sites for Sam68.
source: The canonical PAS sequences (AAUAAA and AUUAAA) correspond to optimal binding sites for Sam68 (Ray et al., 2013; Feracci et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Ray et al., 2013; Feracci et al., 2016).

claim: Stem cells often rely on anaerobic glycolysis for their proliferation and self-renewal.
source: Stem cells often rely on anaerobic glycolysis for their proliferation and self-renewal (Ito and Suda, 2014) and high glycolytic activity is required to prevent precocious NPC differentiation in vivo (Lange et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Ito and Suda, 2014).

claim: High glycolytic activity is required to prevent precocious NPC differentiation in vivo.
source: Stem cells often rely on anaerobic glycolysis for their proliferation and self-renewal (Ito and Suda, 2014) and high glycolytic activity is required to prevent precocious NPC differentiation in vivo (Lange et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Lange et al., 2016).

claim: ALDH1A3 is involved in the glycolytic metabolic pathway.
source: Since ALDH1A3 is involved in this metabolic pathway (Mao et al., 2013), we investigated whether Sam68 expression affects anaerobic glycolysis in NPCs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Mao et al., 2013).

claim: ALDH1A3 promotes self-renewal and clonogenic potential of glioma stem cells.
source: ALDH1A3 was shown to support clonogenicity and tumorigenicity of glioma stem cells by enhancing the glycolytic pathway (Mao et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Mao et al., 2013).

claim: Anaerobic glycolysis is required for NPC self-renewal in vivo.
source: Notably, very recent studies demonstrated that anaerobic glycolysis is required for NPC self-renewal in vivo (Lange et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature (Lange et al., 2016).

claim: Altered neurogenesis and cortical development are associated with severe neuronal disorders like epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism.
source: Since altered neurogenesis and cortical development are associated to severe neuronal disorders like epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism (Sun and Hevner, 2014; Fernández et al., 2016), our findings suggest that fine-tuned regulation of Sam68 expression represents a safeguard mechanism during brain development.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature (Sun and Hevner, 2014; Fernández et al., 2016).

claim: Sam68 binding is required to mask the cryptic PAS and avoid premature termination of the Aldh1a3 transcript in mouse NPCs.
source: These observations strongly suggest that Sam68 binding is required to mask the cryptic PAS and avoid premature termination of the Aldh1a3 transcript in mouse NPCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CLIP data showing Sam68 binding to the cryptic PAS and the 3'-RACE data showing premature termination in knockout cells.

claim: Alternative 3'-end processing of the Aldh1a3 transcript is a physiological process of NPC differentiation controlled by fluctuations in Sam68 expression.
source: Importantly, this decline was accompanied by reduced Sam68 expression and increased expression of ALDH1A3△ (Figure 6D), indicating that alternative 3'-end processing of the Aldh1a3 transcript is a physiological process of NPC differentiation controlled by fluctuations in Sam68 expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Sam68 and full-length Aldh1a3 decline together during differentiation while the truncated form increases.

claim: Sam68 is required to promote the expression and activity of ALDH1A3 through modulation of its pre-mRNA 3'-end processing in both embryonic and post-natal mouse brain.
source: These results indicate that Sam68 is required to promote the expression and activity of ALDH1A3 through modulation of its pre-mRNA 3'-end processing in both embryonic and post-natal mouse brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing Sam68 regulation of Aldh1a3 processing in NPCs and in post-natal brain regions.

claim: Sam68 promotes NPC proliferation and represses their differentiation by maintaining high levels of full-length ALDH1A3.
source: Collectively, these results support the notion that Sam68 promotes NPC proliferation and represses their differentiation by maintaining high levels of full-length ALDH1A3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from rescue experiments showing that ALDH1A3 overexpression rescues knockout phenotypes and knockdown mimics them.

claim: Sam68 maintains high levels of anaerobic glycolysis through modulation of ALDH1A3 protein expression.
source: These findings indicate that Sam68 maintains high levels of anaerobic glycolysis through modulation of ALDH1A3 protein expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that ALDH1A3 modulation affects glycolytic metabolism in NPCs.

claim: Sam68-dependent modulation of ALDH1A3 expression is required to maintain self-renewal capacity of NPCs through enhanced glycolytic metabolism.
source: These results strongly indicate that Sam68-dependent modulation of ALDH1A3 expression is required to maintain self-renewal capacity of NPCs through enhanced glycolytic metabolism (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments linking Sam68, ALDH1A3, glycolysis, and NPC self-renewal.

claim: High levels of Sam68 expression are required for the correct processing of Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA during neurogenesis.
source: Our work suggests that during neurogenesis, high levels of Sam68 expression are required for the correct processing of Aldh1a3 pre-mRNA, thus insuring high ALDH1A3 activity and fueling of the glycolytic pathway.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings linking Sam68 expression to Aldh1a3 processing and glycolytic activity.

claim: A decline in Sam68 expression leads to reduced expression and activity of ALDH1A3 and inhibits the glycolytic pathway, priming NPCs to enter the differentiation program.
source: Conversely, a decline in Sam68 expression leads to reduced expression and activity of ALDH1A3 and inhibits the glycolytic pathway, priming NPCs to enter the differentiation program (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings showing that Sam68 decline during differentiation correlates with reduced ALDH1A3 and glycolysis.

claim: The impaired balance between self-renewal and differentiation in Khdrbs1-/- mice results in depletion of the NPC pool and reduced expansion of the neocortex.
source: Importantly, the impaired balance between self-renewal and differentiation in Khdrbs1-/- mice results in depletion of the NPC pool and reduced expansion of the neocortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vivo experiments showing reduced NPC numbers and cortical expansion in knockout embryos.

claim: Fine-tuned regulation of Sam68 expression represents a safeguard mechanism during brain development.
source: Since altered neurogenesis and cortical development are associated to severe neuronal disorders like epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism (Sun and Hevner, 2014; Fernández et al., 2016), our findings suggest that fine-tuned regulation of Sam68 expression represents a safeguard mechanism during brain development.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings about Sam68's role in neurogenesis and the known association of neurogenesis defects with neurological disorders.

claim: Sam68 expression is high in embryonic NPCs and declines upon differentiation.
source: These results suggested that Sam68 expression is high in NPCs and declines upon differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental expression pattern and co-localization with NPC markers.

claim: In the absence of Sam68, NPCs are prone to exit the cell cycle and differentiate.
source: The concomitant decrease in proliferating cells and increase in post-mitotic neurons observed in the knockout embryos suggested that, in the absence of Sam68, NPCs are prone to exit the cell cycle and differentiate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of decreased proliferating cells and increased differentiated neurons in knockout embryos.

claim: Ablation of Sam68 depletes the NPC pool and limits cortical expansion during neurogenesis.
source: These observations strongly suggest that ablation of Sam68 depletes the NPC pool and limits cortical expansion during neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of reduced NPCs and cortical expansion in knockout embryos.

claim: Khdrbs1-/- NPCs display a tendency to lose stemness and differentiate.
source: Collectively, these features suggested that Khdrbs1-/- NPCs display a tendency to lose stemness and differentiate.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological observations and attachment behavior of knockout NPCs.

claim: The reduced self-renewal capacity of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs was due to dysregulation of gene expression.
source: We hypothesized that the reduced self-renewal capacity of Khdrbs1-/- NPCs was due to dysregulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that led to the microarray experiments.

claim: The localization of ALDH1A3 suggests that its expression is restricted to RGCs.
source: The localization of ALDH1A3 suggests that its expression is restricted to RGCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ALDH1A3 staining is restricted to SOX2+ cells in VZ and SVZ.

claim: ALDH1A3△ appears to be either very unstable or not expressed in NPCs.
source: Thus, ALDH1A3△ appears to be either very unstable or not expressed in NPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure to detect the truncated protein by Western blot despite evidence of the truncated transcript.

claim: Even if expressed at low levels, ALDH1A3△ could not contribute to ALDH activity in NPCs, but it could eventually exert a dominant-negative effect.
source: These observations suggest that, even if expressed at low levels, ALDH1A3△ could not contribute to ALDH activity in NPCs, but it could eventually exert a dominant-negative effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that ALDH1A3△ is inactive and reduces activity of full-length ALDH1A3 when co-expressed.

claim: The clonogenic potential of both wild-type and knockout NPCs was tightly linked to the extent of glycolysis.
source: Furthermore, the clonogenic potential of both wild-type and knockout NPCs was tightly linked to the extent of glycolysis, as modulation of this metabolic pathway by up- or down-regulating ALDH1A3 activity paralleled their self-renewal potential.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that modulation of ALDH1A3 and glycolysis affects clonogenicity.

claim: Sam68 plays a more restricted role than U1 snRNP in controlling 3'-end processing, affecting only a limited subset of transcripts.
source: However, Sam68 appears to play a much more restricted role than U1 snRNP, by controlling 3'-end processing of only a limited subset of transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Sam68's function to that of U1 snRNP and the observation that Sam68 affects only a small number of genes.
